You are the closing enforcer. A debater's closing round may not contradict what the same debater stated in its earlier rounds. Below are one debater's four rounds.
Read its closing round against its earlier rounds. List every closing sentence that cannot be true together with an earlier sentence, and answer every candidate listed.
A contradiction is two statements that cannot both be true. A closing sentence that asserts again, as the debater's own, what it withdrew, dropped or gave up in an earlier round IS a contradiction.
It is NOT a contradiction when the closing sentence: grants, concedes, narrows or withdraws something; states or quotes the other side's position; answers a press with a further reason the earlier sentence leaves room for; or differs only in wording.
Quote both sentences word for word and name the link: the link whose closing block holds the sentence, else the link the earlier sentence supports.

=== [CR1] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Position.** Christ was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost. Joseph was her husband and the child's guardian, but he was not the one who begat him. No man was his biological father. [L4, resting on the verses below]

## 1. Matthew's genealogy changes its verb at Joseph

[L1] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob, and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren". Every father in the line is named with the active verb "begat".

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

[L2] The verb behind both "begat" and "was born" is gennaō (G1080, to beget; in the passive, to be born). In Matthew 1:16 the active "begat" (egennēsen) stops at Joseph. Joseph is called "the husband of Mary", not the one who begat Jesus. The next verb is the passive egennēthē, "was born". The relative "of whom" is the Greek hēs (feminine singular, "of her"), so the birth is traced to Mary alone.

[L3] Matthew 1:2 shows the pattern the line follows until Joseph. In Matthew 1:16 the pattern is deliberately not continued.

[L4] Matthew keeps "A begat B" through the whole line and then, at Joseph, switches to the passive and a feminine relative. So he is denying that Joseph begat Jesus. This rests on the verb (L2) and the broken pattern (L1, L3).

## 2. The source of the conception is stated: the Holy Ghost

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

[L2] "Of" is ek (G1537, out of, from as source). "Of the Holy Ghost" is ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of the Holy Spirit". "That which is conceived" is gennēthen, the same root verb (G1080) that Matthew 1:2 uses for a father's begetting. Matthew 1:20 therefore gives as the source of the begetting the Holy Ghost, in the place where a human father would stand.

[L3] Matthew 1:18 says this was "before they came together". Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". In Matthew 1:25 "knew" is ginōskō (G1097), used here of marital relations, and "till" is heōs (G2193, until).

[L4] The conception was found before the couple came together (Matthew 1:18), and its stated source is the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20, ek). Joseph's relations with Mary are placed after the birth (Matthew 1:25). Therefore Joseph is excluded as the begetter.

## 3. Mary and the angel, in Luke

[L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph". [L2] "Virgin" is parthenos (G3933, a virgin).

[L1] Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" [L2] "Know" is ginōskō (G1097) and "man" is anēr (G435, a man, a husband).

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

[L2] "Overshadow" is episkiazō (G1982, to cast a shadow over). "Therefore" is dio (G1352, wherefore). The reason he is called the Son of God is the Holy Ghost's action upon Mary.

[L4] Mary asks how it can be, "seeing I know not a man" (Luke 1:34), and the angel answers with the Holy Ghost's coming and the power of the Highest (Luke 1:35). That answer names the means, and it is not a man. It rests on Luke 1:34 (L1) and the sense of episkiazō (L2).

## 4. Joseph's fatherhood is described as supposed

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph". [L2] "Supposed" is enomizeto, from nomizō (G3543, to think, to deem by custom or opinion).

[L3] Pre-emptive answer on the passages that call Joseph "father". Luke 2:48 has Mary say, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing". Luke 2:49 gives the reply: "wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" The child answers with a different Father, in the house where Mary had spoken of Joseph. John 6:42 reports what "they said": "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" That is the crowd's opinion, and it is the same "supposed" of Luke 3:23.

[L4] Luke 3:23 marks the "son of Joseph" label as opinion (L2, nomizō). Luke 2:49 gives the child's own different answer (L1, L3). So the "father" language is legal and household usage, and it does not state who begat him.

## 5. The prophecy and the body prepared

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." [L2] The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" is ha'almah (H5959, the maiden, rendered "virgin" in this verse).

[L1] Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son". [L2] Matthew's word is parthenos (G3933, a virgin).

[L3] Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me". [L2] "Body" is sōma (G4983, a body), and "prepared" is katartizō (G2675, to fit, to make ready).

[L4] Matthew 1:23 applies Isaiah 7:14 to the birth of Jesus (L1, L3). Hebrews 10:5 says the body was prepared (L2, L3), which fits the Holy Ghost's work in Luke 1:35 and not a man's begetting.

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. Matthew breaks his "begat" line at Joseph: Matthew 1:2 and 1:16 [L1]; gennaō (G1080) in the active "begat" ending at Joseph, then the passive egennēthē with the feminine hēs ("of whom", of Mary) [L2]; so Joseph is not named as the begetter of Jesus.
2. The conceiving is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost": Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 [L1]; ek (G1537, out of, as source) with gennēthen (G1080, conceived) [L2]; Matthew 1:25 puts "knew her not" until the birth [L3].
3. Mary and the angel put no man as the cause: Luke 1:34 and 1:35 [L1]; ginōskō (G1097) and episkiazō (G1982, to overshadow) [L2]; Luke 1:27 "a virgin" [L3].
4. The "son of Joseph" and "father" language is opinion or household usage: Luke 3:23 "as was supposed" [L1]; nomizō (G3543, to deem) [L2]; Luke 2:48-49 and John 6:42 [L3].
5. Prophecy and the prepared body fit a virgin conception: Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23 [L1]; ha'almah (H5959) and parthenos (G3933) [L2]; Hebrews 10:5 "a body hast thou prepared me" [L3].
6. Christ had no human biological father: Matthew 1:16 and 1:20, and Luke 1:35 [L1]; gennaō (G1080) with ek (G1537) and episkiazō (G1982) [L2]; Luke 1:34 and Luke 3:23 [L3].

=== [CR2] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# ROUND 2: ANSWER TO THE PRESSES (revised)

I grant what the rows give. Joseph is "her husband" (Matthew 1:19) and the child's guardian. Luke 2:4 names Joseph as "of the house and lineage of David". "Seed of David" and "fruit of his loins" are said of Christ. The question is how that descent reaches him.

## D1: the verb and its object

[L1] Matthew 1:3: "And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar". Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus".

[L2] I grant the challenger's point on ek (G1537, out of). It marks the mother at Matthew 1:3, 5 and 6, so the feminine relative in 1:16 does not by itself remove Joseph. Gennaō (G1080) is "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)". The active "begat" is the father's verb.

[L3] Matthew 1:3, 5 and 6 always give the child as the object of "begat": Judas begat Phares, Booz begat Obed, David begat Solomon. Matthew 1:16 gives "begat" the object "Joseph". Jesus is not its object. He is the subject of the passive "was born", and the one the birth is "of" is Mary.

[L4] Matthew keeps the father's verb with the child as its object through every generation. At Jesus he drops it and gives the passive with Mary alone. This rests on Matthew 1:3, 5, 6 and 16 (L1, L3) and the father/mother senses of G1080 (L2).

**Naming does not mean begetting.**
- [L1] Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". Mary is also told to name him.
- [L3] Genesis 29:32: "Leah conceived, and bare a son, and she called his name Reuben". Luke 1:60: "his mother answered and said, Not so; but he shall be called John". Isaiah 7:14, margin: "thou, O virgin, shalt call".
- [L4] Mothers name children, and so does a guardian who is told to. Joseph's naming in Matthew 1:21 and 1:25 therefore fits a guardian's act as well as a begetter's (L1, L3).

**"Son of David".** [L1] Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife". [L4] The verse states Joseph's own descent and gives it in the same sentence as the command to take Mary, with the reason that follows: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". The descent from David is said of Joseph. The conception is said to be of the Holy Ghost (L1). So the verse shows how the child entered David's house through the husband's taking of Mary (Matthew 1:24).

## D2: the angel's "for" and the timing rows

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". The margin reads "conceived: Gr. begotten".

[L2] The word is gennaō (G1080), the father's verb. The reason (gar, for) Joseph need not fear is that what is begotten in her is ek (G1537, out of) the Holy Ghost.

[L3] Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband... was minded to put her away privily". The word is apolyō (G630, to dismiss or divorce). Matthew 1:20 says "while he thought on these things", with enthymeomai (G1760, to ponder).

[L4] Joseph's reaction was to put her away (L1, L3). A reason that quiets that fear is a begetter other than himself. If Joseph were the begetter, the "for" clause would give him nothing to answer his fear. Matthew 1:20's "for" stands on this ground (L1, L2).

**The birth verbs.**
- [L1] John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God".
- [L2] Gennaō in the figurative sense is "to regenerate" (G1080).
- [L3] John 3:6: "that which is born of the Spirit is spirit". 1 John 5:1: "is born of God".
- [L4] "Born of God" in John 1:13 is set against "of blood" and "the will of man". It is the second birth of believers, and each of them had a first birth by a father (L1, L2, L3). Matthew 1:20 puts God's source on the one conception, in her womb (L1). The challenger's rows compare two births in one person with one conception.

**Timing.**
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost".
- [L2] Synerchomai (G4905) in the lexicon includes "cohabit (conjugally)".
- [L3] Matthew 1:25: "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". [L1] Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived".
- [L4] Genesis 4:1 gives "knew... and she conceived" as one pair. Matthew 1:18 gives "before they came together... found with child of the Holy Ghost", and Matthew 1:25 gives "knew her not till she had brought forth". Her being found with child comes before the coming together, and the not-knowing runs to the birth. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost (L1, L2, L3).

## D3: Luke 1:35

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God".

[L2] I grant that eperchomai (G1904) and episkiazō (G1982) are used elsewhere of power and presence (Acts 1:8, Luke 9:34). Dio (G1352, wherefore) and the result clause tie "that holy thing which shall be born of thee" to those two verbs.

[L3] Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son". Luke 1:35: "shall be born of thee". The angel to Zacharias says "bear thee a son", with the husband in the sentence. The angel to Mary says "of thee", with the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest in the sentence.

[L4] The question was "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (Luke 1:34, L1, with ginōskō G1097, know). The reply gives the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest as the cause of the birth "of thee" (L1, L2). That is the stated means. Elisabeth's sign (Luke 1:36) is a conception "in her old age" in one "who was called barren" (L1), and it answers age and barrenness. Mary's question was "seeing I know not a man", so her sign answers a different matter (L1).

**The throne.** [L1] Luke 1:32: "the throne of his father David". [L4] David is "father" here across the generations, so "father" in Luke 1:32 carries the forefather's sense, which my D6 answer below uses (L1, with Hebrews 7:10 at L3).

## D4: "supposed"

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

[L2] The word is nomizō (G3543). I grant it can mean "wont", as in Acts 16:13.

[L3] Luke 2:44: "But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey". Acts 14:19: "supposing he had been dead". The challenger cited Luke 2:44, and the supposing there proved mistaken. In Acts 14:19 it was also mistaken.

[L4] Luke's own uses of "supposing" in 2:44 and Acts 14:19 are of beliefs that turned out wrong (L1, L3). In Luke 3:23 the parenthesis stands at the one place where "son of Joseph" would otherwise be stated flat, so it carries the same sense.

**Luke 2:33.** [L1] Luke 2:33: "And Joseph and his mother marvelled". The narrator names Joseph by name and attaches "his" to the mother. Luke 2:27 and 2:41 give "parents", which is goneus (G1118, parents of a household). Mary's "thy father" (2:48) is her address. The child answers in the same exchange with "my Father's business" (2:49), and so names a different Father (L1, L3).

**The covenant pattern.** [L3] 2 Samuel 7:14 says "I will be his father" of Solomon, who proceeded "out of thy bowels" (2 Samuel 7:12). Hebrews 1:5 puts the same words to Christ: "I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?" [L4] The 2 Samuel row joins two fathers because Solomon had a human begetter. Hebrews 1:5 applies only the second half of that pairing, "I will be to him a Father", to Christ (L1, L3).

## D5: Hebrews 10:5

[L1] Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me". The margin reads "or, thou hast fitted me".

[L2] Katartizō (G2675) is "to fit, make ready". Its subject is God.

[L3] Hebrews 2:14: "he also himself likewise took part of the same", meaning the flesh of the children.

[L4] I concede D5 is a fit only. Hebrews 10:5 gives God as the preparer of the body, and Hebrews 2:14 gives true flesh (L1, L3). Together they corroborate D1 to D3, and I rest nothing on D5 alone. Isaiah 7:14 stands on its own words: "a virgin shall conceive" (L1), applied in Matthew 1:23 as "a virgin shall be with child" (L3) with parthenos (G3933, a virgin) (L2). Isaiah 8:3 speaks of "the prophetess", and her child is named "Mahershalalhashbaz", a different child from Immanuel (L1, L3).

## D6: the seed, the loins, and Hebrews 7:14

**What "seed" and "loins" carry.**
- [L1] Hebrews 7:10: "he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him".
- [L3] Hebrews 7:9: "Levi... payed tithes in Abraham". The loins that carried Levi were Abraham's, his forefather's, three generations back.
- [L3] Genesis 35:11: "kings shall come out of thy loins". This is said to Jacob of a line of descendants.
- [L2] Osphys (G3751) is the loin. Sperma (G4690) is "seed (including the male 'sperm'); by implication, offspring". Zera' (H2233) is seed.
- [L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed". The woman has "seed".
- [L4] "Loins of his father" in Hebrews 7:10 spans generations (L1, L3). "Seed" is a woman's offspring in Genesis 3:15 (L3) and "offspring" in G4690 (L2). Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30 and 2 Timothy 2:8 each state descent "of the seed of David", and a mother's seed fits those words as Genesis 3:15 shows. Romans 1:3 says "made" (ginomai, G1096, come into being) and not "begotten" (L1, L2).

**My answer to the question on Hebrews 7:14.** [L1] Hebrews 7:14: "it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda".

[L3] The evident record is twofold. The legal house comes through Joseph: Luke 2:4, "of the house and lineage of David", and Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David". Joseph took Mary and named the child (Matthew 1:24-25). Numbers 1:18 registers "by the house of their fathers".

[L3] The flesh comes from David by descent. Matthew 1:16 says "Jacob begat Joseph". Luke 3:23 says "the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli". The KJV prints "the son" in italics in that clause, so it is supplied. Ezra 2:61 shows a man who "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai... and was called after their name".

[L4] Two names for Joseph's father, Jacob and Heli, stand in Matthew 1:16 and Luke 3:23. Ezra 2:61 shows a man reckoned by his wife's father's name (L3). Romans 1:3 gives the seed of David as "offspring" in G4690 (L2), and Genesis 3:15 gives a woman her "seed" (L3). I mark this reading as an [L4] on those layers: the flesh of David's seed came to the child through Mary, and the legal house of Luke 2:4 is Joseph's, registered to the Hebrews' readers through him.

**A question to the challenger.** In Matthew 1:20 the angel gives as the reason Joseph should not fear taking Mary: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". If Joseph was the begetter, what work does that "for" do?

=== [CR3] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 3, LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: SUPPORTED**

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
[L2] gennaō (G1080, to procreate, properly of the father, by extension of the mother) stands in both halves of the verse. It is active, "begat," up to Joseph. The relative "of whom" is feminine singular, and the verb then turns passive, "was born."
[L3] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren". Matthew 1:7-15 carries the same "begat" form unbroken from Solomon to Jacob.
[L4] The chain of "begat" ends with Jacob begetting Joseph. The next verb is the passive, and its only subject is the woman. Joseph is given as "the husband of Mary" and is not given a begetting verb. This rests on [L1] 1:16 and 1:2 and on [L2] G1080.

Answers to the presses:
- Matthew 1:3, "And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar," Matthew 1:5, "And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth," and Matthew 1:6, "David the king begat Solomon of her [that had been the wife] of Urias." In each of these a father's active "begat" stands before the woman's "of." In 1:16 the active "begat" stops at Joseph, and the one born is introduced by "was born" with the woman alone. The challenger's own rows show the formula that 1:16 leaves.
- Matthew 1:1, "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham," and Matthew 1:17, "from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ [are] fourteen generations." I grant both. Matthew 1:20 calls Joseph "thou son of David." The heading names the child's descent. The verb of 1:16 that follows Joseph is "was born," with the woman. Romans 1:3 gives the flesh the verb "made" (ginomai, G1096, to become): "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- Matthew 1:21, "and thou shalt call his name JESUS," Matthew 1:25, "and he called his name JESUS," and Luke 1:62, "they made signs to his father, how he would have him called." Naming is a parent's act in either direction. Genesis 29:32 has Leah naming: "she called his name Reuben." Luke 1:60 has the mother naming: "he shall be called John." Luke 1:13 reads "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John." Matthew 1:21 reads "she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS." The words "bear thee" stand in the first, and Matthew 1:21 reads "she shall bring forth a son."

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source of what was conceived in Mary before she and Joseph came together, and Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:25 bear that out. I drop any reliance on 1 John 5:1 as a proof.

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
[L2] synerchomai (G4905) includes "cohabit (conjugally)." The finding therefore stands before the cohabiting.
[L1] Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
[L2] gennaō (G1080) is the verb of the begetter. Here it is passive, "that which is begotten in her," and the source is ek pneumatos hagiou (G4151, G40: out of the spirit, holy).
[L3] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
[L4] The "of the Holy Ghost" source is stated before the taking in 1:24. This rests on [L1] 1:18 and 1:20 and on [L2] G4905 and G1080. Joseph's part is then "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."

Answers to the presses:
- Matthew 1:20 with gar (G1063, for). The "for" gives the ground for the command: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The ground stated is the source of the conception.
- 1 Chronicles 28:6: "for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father." There the ground is God's choice ("chosen"). In Matthew 1:20 the ground is what was begotten in her. 1 Chronicles 28:6 is spoken to a father about a son he begat, and it does not carry over, so I drop it.
- 1 John 5:1 and Romans 1:3. I grant that "born of God" in 1 John 5:1 is said of men who have fathers. John 1:13 sets "of God" against "of the will of man": "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." Romans 1:3 reads "made of the seed of David," and its verb is ginomai (G1096, to become).
- Matthew 1:24, "and took unto him his wife," Matthew 1:19, "Then Joseph her husband," and Deuteronomy 22:24, "because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife." I grant that a betrothed is called a wife and husband. Matthew 1:18 still puts the finding "before they came together." Matthew 1:19 records that this husband, "being a just [man]," was "minded to put her away privily."
- Matthew 1:25 and Genesis 4:1. Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." Matthew 1:25 uses the same verb negated, ginōskō (G1097, to know): "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." Matthew 1:20, with the conception already "in her," precedes the taking in 1:24. Heōs (G2193, until) therefore runs to the birth, over the time of conception.

**LINK 3: SUPPORTED**

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
